passage:
Reena,
I owe you an apology for the email I sent at four yesterday. Reading it again this morning, it was harsh and unfair. 'This is unacceptable' was not the way to point out a delay in your section.
Here's the honest background. I skipped lunch to finish the audit report, drank three cups of tea instead, and by four everything looked like a disaster: the delay, the project, my whole career. I remember thinking we'd never fix it. Then I ate a samosa at six, and suddenly it looked like a two-day slip we can easily recover.
I've set a lunch alarm now. Can we talk this afternoon, after I've eaten?
Madhav

qa.q: What did Madhav drink instead of eating lunch?
qa.a: Three cups of tea.

qa.q: How did Madhav feel about work by four o'clock?
qa.a: Madhav felt hopeless and alarmed, as if the delay meant the whole project and career were a disaster.

qa.q: What is Madhav doing differently now?
qa.a: Keeping a lunch alarm and choosing to talk after eating, when problems look their true size.

qa.q: How might Reena have felt on receiving the 'unacceptable' email?
qa.a: Reena probably felt hurt and unfairly blamed for a small, fixable delay.

grounding: A busy professional skips lunch, writes a harsh email and feels hopeless, then sees how low fuel made problems look bigger.

passage: Himani, you asked how Priyanka and I stopped fighting on Sunday evenings. Honestly? Food. I'm Divyansh, the guy who used to start the week's household talk at eight, starving, after cricket. Every time, my voice got an edge and we ended up shouting about whose fault the electricity bill was. One Sunday I heard that edge mid-sentence. I stopped and said, 'Give me twenty minutes. I'm starving.' I made poha, we ate in front of a silly film, and at nine we sat down again. Same bill, calm talk. But I don't use hunger as an excuse either. When I've been rude, I apologise after the meal. Every time.

qa.q: What did Divyansh make after pausing?
qa.a: Poha.

qa.q: What did Divyansh notice mid-sentence, and how did it feel?
qa.a: Divyansh heard the edge in that sentence and felt alarmed that hunger was steering the talk towards a fight.

qa.q: Why doesn't Divyansh use hunger as an excuse?
qa.a: Eating first prevents fights, but rudeness still needs an apology after the meal, so the habit protects the relationship without excusing it.

qa.q: How might Priyanka experience the new Sunday evenings?
qa.a: Priyanka probably feels calmer and more respected, able to discuss the bill without being shouted at.

grounding: A person notices the edge in their own voice, eats first and returns to the hard talk later, still apologising for rudeness.

passage:
'Francis, she's whining again. She won't play, won't eat.'
'Maybe she's sleepy? She's rubbing her eyes.'
'She napped an hour ago. Look how she's clinging to me.'
'When did she last drink anything?'
Pema paused. 'The juice at breakfast. We've been on the beach all morning.'
'In this heat? Give her the water bottle.'
Little Anya gulped and gulped, water dribbling down her chin.
'Oh, baby, you were thirsty.'
Ten minutes later Anya was back on the sand, patting a castle.

qa.q: When did Anya last drink before the water?
qa.a: The juice at breakfast.

qa.q: Why was Anya whining and clinging?
qa.a: She was thirsty and uncomfortable in the heat but couldn't say so, so she felt fussy and clingy.

qa.q: What simple step helped Anya?
qa.a: Offering her water; after gulping it she went back to playing.

qa.q: How might Pema feel on realising Anya was thirsty?
qa.a: Pema may feel a pang of guilt at forgetting water on a hot morning, and relief that the fix was simple.

grounding: A toddler short of water on a hot day becomes fussy and clingy, and offering water rescues her mood.

passage: Sunaina, don't leave your bottle on the table again. Let your grandfather Tenzin tell you why. When I was about your age, at the school in Kalimpong, I loved football more than food. One hot May day I played the whole lunch break, forgot my water, and by afternoon my head was pounding. I was so grumpy that I tore my friend Dawa's drawing when he laughed at me. The teacher sat me in the shade with a jug of water and asked, 'When did you drink today?' I couldn't remember. Slowly the headache faded, and I felt terrible about the drawing. From then on I tied my bottle to my bag strap and drank before every match.

qa.q: Where did young Tenzin tie the bottle?
qa.a: To the bag strap.

qa.q: How did young Tenzin feel in the afternoon after the match?
qa.a: He felt grumpy and sore-headed, so irritable that he tore Dawa's drawing.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Tenzin's story?
qa.a: The teacher sitting him in the shade with water and asking when he'd drunk; after that he carried his bottle and drank before matches.

qa.q: How might Dawa have felt when the drawing was torn?
qa.a: Dawa probably felt hurt and shocked, since he had only laughed.

grounding: A grandfather recalls forgetting water while playing in the sun as a schoolchild and learning to notice thirst.

subtype: Sports practice fatigue and short temper [Observer]
passage:
Coach's log, under-16 girls' hockey, Thursday
Swati is normally first on the field, cheering everyone. Today, after ninety minutes of drills in the afternoon sun, she was dragging her stick, missing easy passes, and she snapped at her captain, 'Just leave me alone!' My first instinct was a pep talk to the whole team about attitude. Then I realised nobody had taken a water break since the warm-up, and her bottle sat still full on the bench. I stopped practice and sent everyone into the shade to drink and rest for ten minutes. When we restarted, Swati was calling for the ball again. From now on: water breaks every twenty minutes in the heat.
Zubin

qa.q: Where was Swati's bottle?
qa.a: Still full on the bench.

qa.q: What was Zubin's first instinct, and what did Zubin feel on noticing the full bottle?
qa.a: Zubin's first instinct was a pep talk about attitude, then Zubin felt concerned on seeing no one had had a water break.

qa.q: What rule did Zubin make?
qa.a: Water breaks every twenty minutes in the heat.

qa.q: What was practice like for Swati before the break?
qa.a: She was probably exhausted and irritable from heat and thirst, so every pass and word felt like too much.

grounding: A coach sees a keen teenager turn slow and sharp after training in heat without water and uses water breaks, not a pep talk.

subtype: Mistaking thirst for tiredness or hunger [Actor]
passage: By three o'clock in the Bengaluru co-working space, Chinmay's brain felt like wet cotton. He'd had two cups of filter coffee, a packet of chips and a cream biscuit, and still the spreadsheet swam. He was reaching for a fourth snack when Parul, at the next desk, set down a steel tumbler of water. 'You haven't touched your bottle all day. It's still full.' He drank the tumbler, then half the bottle, and stepped out onto the terrace for five minutes. When he came back, the columns made sense again. 'I thought I was hungry,' he admitted. 'Or tired.' Parul shrugged. 'Sometimes it's just water.'

qa.q: What did Parul set down for Chinmay?
qa.a: A steel tumbler of water.

qa.q: What did Chinmay think was wrong with him?
qa.a: He felt foggy and sluggish and assumed he was hungry or tired, so he kept reaching for coffee and snacks.

qa.q: What cleared Chinmay's fog?
qa.a: Water and a five-minute break on the terrace.

qa.q: How might Parul have seen Chinmay's afternoon?
qa.a: Parul noticed the full bottle and the snacking, and was probably amused but caring enough to bring water.

grounding: A young adult mistakes thirst for hunger or tiredness until water and a short break clear the fog.

passage:
'Another headache?' Rafiq asked as Damini dropped her bag.
'This job is killing me. Everyone's an idiot today. I nearly cried in the review.'
'What did you drink today?'
'Tea. Coffee. Tea again. Why?'
'Any water?'
'I don't have time for water, Rafiq. I have deadlines.'
'No time to walk to the cooler, but time for three cups of tea and coffee?'
She glared, then laughed despite herself. 'Fine. Tomorrow I'll try.'
Next evening she came home humming. 'Filled my bottle three times. No headache. And the team seemed half as stupid.'
'Funny how that works.'
'Don't be smug.'

qa.q: What had Damini drunk that day?
qa.a: Tea, coffee, and tea again.

qa.q: How was Damini feeling when she came home?
qa.a: She felt irritable and low, with a headache, blaming the job and having nearly cried in the review.

qa.q: What small habit changed Damini's next day?
qa.a: Filling her water bottle three times, which left her without a headache and more patient.

qa.q: How might Rafiq feel seeing Damini come home humming?
qa.a: Rafiq likely felt pleased and a little smug that such a small change helped.

grounding: A professional drinking only tea and coffee blames the job for her headache and mood until regular water helps.

passage: For a month Anders had been dragging himself through his job at the Oslo shipping office. He drank water constantly and was still thirsty, went to bed early and still woke up exhausted. He tried cutting sugar, walking at lunch, sleeping more. Nothing changed. 'Maybe I'm just lazy,' he told his sister Olga over dinner. Olga put down her fork. 'Lazy people aren't thirsty all day. That's your body saying something. Book a doctor.' Anders hesitated; he hated fuss. But the next morning he called the clinic, got an appointment for Thursday, and wrote down everything he'd noticed so he wouldn't forget.

qa.q: When was Anders's appointment?
qa.a: Thursday.

qa.q: Why did Anders hesitate before booking the doctor?
qa.a: He felt reluctant to make a fuss and half-believed he was just lazy.

qa.q: What made Anders's response a sensible one?
qa.a: When rest and small changes didn't help, he booked a doctor and wrote down what he'd noticed instead of guessing.

qa.q: How did Olga see Anders's tiredness?
qa.a: Olga felt concerned and saw it as a body signal, not laziness, so she urged a doctor.

grounding: A young man with ongoing tiredness and thirst despite rest stops guessing and sees a doctor.

passage: In the village near Moga, little Varun, usually happy chasing hens, cried all afternoon. He pushed away his roti, clung to Gurpreet's dupatta and woke screaming from his nap. Gurpreet's mother-in-law said, 'Spoilt, that's all.' But Gurpreet noticed him tugging at his right ear and turning his face into her shoulder. 'Something hurts,' she said. That evening she carried him to the health centre in the next village, where the doctor was still seeing patients. Varun slept on her shoulder all the way home.

qa.q: Which ear was Varun tugging?
qa.a: His right ear.

qa.q: What did Varun's crying and clinging suggest he was feeling?
qa.a: He was in pain and upset but couldn't say it, so he cried, refused food and clung for comfort.

qa.q: Why was Gurpreet right to take Varun to the doctor?
qa.a: The sudden mood change and ear tugging were clues that something hurt, and a doctor could check it.

qa.q: How did the mother-in-law see Varun's crying?
qa.a: She saw a spoilt child, missing the signs that Varun was in pain.

grounding: A toddler with ear pain cannot name it and shows it through crying, refusing food and clinging.

subtype: Child hiding pain to avoid fuss [Actor]
passage:
'Shankar, why aren't you eating your payasam? It's your favourite.'
'Not hungry, Appa.'
'And why did you shout at your sister?'
'She keeps talking!'
'You didn't go to cricket either. What's going on?'
Silence. Shankar pressed his hand to his cheek.
'Is it your tooth?'
'No!' Then, very small: 'If I say, you'll take me to the dentist and he'll give an injection. And I'll miss the school trip.'
Harish sat down next to him. 'I'm glad you told me. We'll go to the dentist tomorrow, and I'll stay with you the whole time. Toothaches don't go away by hiding. I'd rather you went on the trip without pain.'
Shankar leaned into him, eyes wet.

qa.q: What did Shankar press his hand to?
qa.a: His cheek.

qa.q: What was Shankar afraid of that made him hide the pain?
qa.a: He was scared of an injection at the dentist and worried about missing the school trip.

qa.q: What did Harish say that made it easier for Shankar?
qa.a: He said he was glad Shankar told him, promised to stay with him at the dentist, and explained that hiding wouldn't make it go away.

qa.q: How might Shankar's sister have felt when he shouted?
qa.a: She probably felt hurt and confused, not knowing his short temper came from a sore tooth.

grounding: A schoolchild hides a toothache for fear of injections and missing a trip, and the pain leaks out as short temper.
